summary: Defines two new IPv4 Options used only with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv4 (ILNPv4), an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: An IPv4 packet has room for extra labels. This memo adds two special labels that only ILNP uses. It is only an experiment.

questions: what ip options does ilnp use
what are the two ilnpv4 ipv4 options
how does ilnpv4 carry identifiers in ipv4
why use ipv4 options instead of extension headers
subtitle: IPv4 header options that carry ILNP identifiers and nonces for security.

tldr.problem: ILNP for IPv4 needs to carry Identifiers (64-bit node names) in packets, but IPv4 headers cannot fit them. It also needs a security nonce to prevent off-path attackers from forging ILNP messages.
tldr.mechanism: Two new IPv4 options using the same experimental option number (158) carry the Identifier values and a cryptographically random 64-bit nonce. Each option is flagged to be copied on fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: This proposal enables ILNPv4 to function similarly to ILNPv6, though using IPv4's option mechanism instead of extension headers due to router silicon constraints.

today: RFC 6746 is an Experimental protocol from the IRTF Routing Research Group published in November 2012. It remains experimental and undeployed as ILNP has not been adopted.

sections.title: Why ILNP Needs New IPv4 Options
sections.content:
In the ILNP architecture, each node is identified by two pieces of information: a Locator (used for routing) and an Identifier (which names the node). In ILNP for IPv6, both fit naturally into the IPv6 header structure. However, IPv4 headers are too small to carry the 64-bit Identifier alongside the 32-bit Locator.

Instead of using IPv6-style extension headers (which modern router silicon cannot parse at line rate), ILNPv4 uses IPv4 Options. Currently deployed routers can parse past IPv4 Options efficiently, so this choice maintains performance.

Additionally, ILNP requires a Nonce—a cryptographically random value that is unique per communication direction—to prevent off-path attackers from forging ICMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 packets have a place for extra information called options. ILNP uses two of them: one for your real identifier (your name) and one for a secret number that proves you are really you.

sections.title: The Two ILNP IPv4 Options
sections.content:
Both options share a single experimental IPv4 Option Type value of 158 (from RFC 4727). To distinguish which option is which, each carries an 8-bit field called ILNPv4_OPT:

  • Option 0x01: ILNP Identifier Option carries the Source Identifier (64 bits) and Destination Identifier (64 bits), for a total of 20 octets including the option header.
  • Option 0x02: ILNP Nonce Option carries a 64-bit nonce value, for a total of 8 octets including the option header.

Both options use Option Class 0 (control) and must be copied upon fragmentation. A packet following RFC 791 byte boundaries would show them in this order: standard IPv4 header, Identifier Option, Nonce Option, then the payload.

Note that Option Type 158 is shared experimental space. Other experiments might use the same value for entirely different purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Both options live in the same space (Type 158), but they have different purposes. Option 1 says "I am Alice" and Option 2 says "and here is my secret number."

sections.title: The ILNP Identifier Option
sections.content:
The Identifier Option carries two 64-bit unsigned integers:

  • Source Identifier: The node sending this packet.
  • Destination Identifier: The node receiving this packet.

These use the same syntax and semantics as ILNP Identifiers in IPv6 and are typically based on modified EUI-64 format. RFC 6741 specifies how to generate valid Identifier values.

The option has Option Length 20, using 4 words as specified in RFC 791. This option MUST NOT appear in an IPv4 packet unless that packet is part of an active ILNPv4 session. The first few packets of each session MUST include this option, and implementations SHOULD include it in all packets if packet loss is high.
sections.plainLanguage: This option is like putting your name and your friend's name on the envelope. It is 16 bytes of information (two 8-byte names).

sections.title: The ILNP Nonce Option
sections.content:
The Nonce Option carries a single 64-bit ILNP Nonce value. The nonce must be:

  • Cryptographically random: Guidance on generating cryptographically random values is in RFC 4086.
  • Unidirectional: The nonce from Alice to Bob is different from the nonce from Bob to Alice. In a TCP session, for example, there are two nonces in use simultaneously.
  • Unpredictable: If an attacker can guess the next nonce value, they might forge messages.

The nonce provides non-cryptographic protection against off-path attacks (attackers not on the network path). An on-link attacker can still observe nonces, but off-path attackers cannot. This is especially useful for protecting ILNP ICMP Locator Update messages.

This option has Option Length 2, occupying 8 octets total. Like the Identifier Option, it MUST NOT appear unless in an ILNPv4 session, and MUST be included in the first few packets of each session and in all ICMP messages generated by ILNP participants.
sections.plainLanguage: This option is a secret number that only you and your friend know. Hackers on the internet cannot see it, so they cannot fake messages pretending to be you.

sections.title: Security Implications and Threats
sections.content:
If the Nonce value becomes predictable, an off-path attacker might forge data or control packets. However, this risk is mitigated by IP Source Address filtering (BCP 38, RFC 2827 and BCP 84, RFC 3704), which is now standard practice.

IPsec (RFC 4301) provides cryptographic protection and can be used in addition to these nonces for deployments in high-threat environments. The nonce is intended for end-to-end use between source and destination nodes.

Modern IPv4 routers often filter out IPv4 options as a defense against DoS attacks. This could prevent ILNPv4 packets from traversing such routers. Implementations must be aware of this operational limitation.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce prevents someone on the internet from lying about messages. Real encryption (IPsec) can add even more protection if you really need it.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
IPv4 nodes that do not support ILNP will simply forward packets containing these options as they would any other IPv4 option, or potentially drop them if the router is configured to filter options. This design maintains backwards compatibility.

If the IETF were to standardize ILNP in the future, allocating unique option type values (separate from the shared experimental 158) would be appropriate. For now, implementations should code defensively, knowing that other experiments might use Option Type 158 for different purposes.

This is an experimental protocol from the IRTF Routing Research Group, intended for research and evaluation only.
sections.plainLanguage: Old computers that do not understand ILNP just pass the packets along. Routers that filter options might drop ILNP packets, which is a deployment challenge.

fields.desc: Length in 32-bit words including type and length; 20 octets = 5 words

fields.desc: Upper 32 bits of a 64-bit cryptographic nonce

fields.desc: Lower 32 bits of a 64-bit cryptographic nonce
